recipes.name: Hanoi Bánh Gối
recipes.description: Hanoi bánh gối is a crisp, pillow-shaped pastry filled with minced pork, wood-ear mushroom, glass noodles and quail egg. This Bếp Việt home batch cools and drains the filling before sealing and frying.
recipes.serving_basis: About 8 pork-filled pastries served with fresh greens and dipping sauce.
recipes.finished_dish: The pastry is golden and crisp, with a soft pork, mushroom and noodle filling and a quail egg inside.
recipes.serving: Serve hot with fresh greens, green papaya pickles and sweet-sour fish sauce.
tips: Cool and drain the filling before wrapping.
Seal the edges firmly; dab dry pastry with a little water.
Fry over medium heat so the shell crisps while the filling cooks through.
recipes.image_alt: Golden Hanoi bánh gối cut open to show pork, mushroom, glass noodles and quail egg, with greens; transparent background.
recipes.time_note: About 1 hour 10 minutes, including 20 minutes for the dough to rest.
search_terms: wood-ear mushroom and glass noodle pastry
preparation_steps: Combine flour and salt; add warm water and oil gradually and knead until smooth. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Soak mushrooms and noodles; mince the mushrooms and cut the noodles. Boil and peel the quail eggs; prepare the greens and papaya.
Prepare the sweet-sour dipping sauce and papaya pickles; drain the ingredients well.
cooking_steps: Sauté shallot, add pork and break it up. Season with fish sauce, sugar and pepper; add carrot, mushrooms and noodles and cook until dry. Cool.
Divide dough into 8 pieces and roll into thin rounds. Add filling and one quail egg, fold into a half-moon and crimp closed.
Fry in batches at about 165–170°C until crisp and golden and the filling is cooked. Drain on paper towels.
Serve hot with greens, pickles and dipping sauce.

recipes.name: Hanoi Rice Noodle Soup with Taro Stems
recipes.description: This Hanoi bowl pairs a light broth with tender pork hock, wood-ear meatballs and crisp taro stems. Bếp Việt’s home recipe explains how to salt, squeeze and rinse the stems to reduce their itchy sensation.
recipes.serving_basis: Four bowls of rice noodles with pork, meatballs and clear broth.
recipes.finished_dish: The broth is clear and balanced; the pork is tender, the meatballs savory and the taro stems crisp without an itchy afterfeel.
recipes.serving: Briefly blanch the noodles, arrange the pork and meatballs, ladle over hot broth and finish with scallion, culantro and cilantro.
tips: Wear gloves when handling taro stems if your skin is sensitive; salt, squeeze and rinse them several times.
Blanch the bones and pork hock before simmering, and skim regularly for a clear broth.
Blanch the taro stems only until just tender; prolonged cooking removes their crisp texture.
recipes.image_alt: A bowl of Hanoi rice noodles with taro stems, pork hock, pork meatballs and clear broth.
recipes.time_note: A gentle simmer keeps the broth clear; salt and rinse the taro stems thoroughly before cooking.
keywords: Hanoi Rice Noodle Soup with Taro Stems
Hanoi Rice Noodle Soup with Taro Stems

ingredients: Choose a piece with both lean meat and skin.
Peel the fibrous outer layer, slice diagonally and prepare thoroughly.
Divide between the taro stems and broth.
preparation_steps: Blanch the pork hock and ribs in boiling water for 2–3 minutes, rinse off the foam and drain.
Peel the fibrous outer layer from the taro stems and slice diagonally. Add about 5 g salt, gently massage, rest for 10 minutes, squeeze dry, then rinse and squeeze again 2–3 times.
Soak the mushrooms in warm water for about 20 minutes, then chop them. Mix the pork paste with the mushrooms and pepper, then shape into small balls.
Wash the scallion, culantro and cilantro; cut the tomato into wedges.
cooking_steps: Put the pork hock, ribs and water in a pot. Bring to a boil, skim, add shallot and remaining salt, then simmer gently for about 40 minutes until tender.
Add the meatballs and cook for 5–7 minutes until they float and are cooked through. Remove and slice the hock; season the broth with fish sauce.
If using tomato, sauté it briefly in a little oil and add it to the pot. Blanch the taro stems in the simmering broth for 1–2 minutes, removing them as soon as tender.
Blanch the noodles and divide among bowls. Arrange the pork, meatballs and taro stems, ladle over hot broth and garnish with scallion, culantro and cilantro.

recipes.name: Giong Luong Coconut Leaf Cake from Ben Tre
recipes.description: Giong Luong cake is wrapped in young nipa palm leaves and combines chewy sticky rice with coconut, black beans and ripe banana. Bếp Việt adapts the long-standing Thạnh Phú craft for a small home batch; wrapping and extended steaming take patience.
recipes.finished_dish: Golden-green leaves enclose tender sticky rice with nutty black beans, ripe banana and a gentle coconut aroma.
recipes.serving: Let the parcels cool slightly, unwrap and serve whole or sliced; best eaten the day they are made.
tips: Soak the sticky rice long enough and drain it thoroughly so the cake cooks chewy rather than wet.
Wipe the young nipa leaves clean, roll them into sealed tubes and tie firmly to keep water out.
Steam for the full time; for larger or thicker parcels, check the center before turning off the heat.
recipes.image_alt: Giong Luong coconut leaf cake wrapped in young nipa leaves, with one parcel opened to show sticky rice, coconut, black beans and banana.
recipes.time_note: This recipe keeps the extended steaming time documented for the traditional craft; actual time varies with parcel thickness.

keywords: Giong Luong Coconut Leaf Cake from Ben Tre
Ben Tre nipa palm leaf cake

ingredients: Rinse, soak for 4 hours and drain.
Soak for 4 hours and boil until nearly tender.
Choose semi-mature coconut, not too old.
Peel and cut into small pieces.
Add a little water if needed.
Wipe clean, soften and use to wrap the cakes.
preparation_steps: Rinse the sticky rice, soak it in clean water for about 4 hours, rinse again and drain completely.
Soak the black beans for 4 hours and boil until nearly tender while keeping the beans intact; drain.
Mix the rice with grated coconut, coconut milk, sugar and salt. Cut the ripe banana into small pieces.
Wipe the nipa leaves clean and roll each into a tube sealed at one end. Layer in rice, beans and a few banana pieces, cover with more rice, fold closed and tie firmly.
cooking_steps: Arrange the parcels in a steamer with a little space between them for steam to circulate.
Bring the water to a boil and steam continuously for about 4–5 hours; add boiling water to the pot as needed and do not let it run dry.
Check one parcel: the leaves should be softened, the rice translucent and chewy, and the beans tender. Let the cakes cool slightly before slicing.

recipes.name: Savory Quán Gánh Bánh Dày
recipes.description: Quán Gánh bánh dày is a well-known sticky-rice cake from Thường Tín, Hanoi. This Bếp Việt savory version combines pounded sticky rice with mung bean and pork filling, wrapped in banana leaf.
recipes.serving_basis: Eight savory bánh dày cakes wrapped in banana leaf, for four people.
recipes.finished_dish: Smooth, chewy white sticky rice surrounds a nutty mung-bean and savory pork filling with a light banana-leaf aroma.
recipes.serving: Serve warm or at room temperature; unwrap the banana leaf to eat.
tips: Soak the rice thoroughly and pound it while hot so it binds.
Oil your hands lightly to prevent sticking.
recipes.image_alt: White Quán Gánh bánh dày in banana leaves, one cut open to show mung bean and pork filling; transparent background.
recipes.time_note: About 5 hours 20 minutes, mostly soaking time for rice and beans.
preparation_steps: Rinse and soak sticky rice for 4 hours. Soak mung beans separately for about 2 hours, then drain.
Steam mung beans until soft and mash. Blanch banana leaves, dry and cut into pieces.
Mince the pork and shallot; dice the fat. Prepare a mortar or masher for the hot rice.
cooking_steps: Fry shallot in pork fat, add pork and cook through. Season with fish sauce, pepper and some salt; mix with mashed mung beans, cool and divide into 8 portions.
Steam rice with remaining salt for 35–40 minutes until tender and sticky. While hot, pound or mash until smooth and cohesive.
Divide rice into 8 portions, flatten, add filling and seal. Shape into rounds and wrap each cake in banana leaf.
Serve warm or let cool briefly to set.

recipes.name: Northern Vietnamese Rice Balls with Sesame Salt
recipes.description: Warm rice is pressed into a tender, chewy roll and served with nutty toasted sesame salt, a humble countryside food from northern Vietnam. Bếp Việt keeps the method simple and explains how to cook rice that binds well and shape it while warm.
recipes.serving_basis: Four servings of rice balls with sesame salt, for breakfast or a packed meal.
recipes.finished_dish: The rice holds together while staying soft and chewy; the sesame salt is fragrant, nutty and mildly salty, with optional roasted peanuts.
recipes.serving: Slice the rice roll with a slightly wet knife or clean thread and dip into sesame salt while still warm.
tips: Choose a moderately sticky rice and cook it so it is neither dry nor mushy.
Shape the rice while warm using a clean cloth or food-safe plastic wrap.
Toast sesame over low heat, stirring constantly; turn off the heat as soon as fragrant to prevent bitterness.
recipes.image_alt: Slices of a white rice roll served with a small bowl of toasted sesame and peanut salt.
recipes.time_note: Rice-cooking time varies by grain and cooker; avoid shaping the rice while it is too hot to handle safely.
keywords: Northern Vietnamese Rice Balls with Sesame Salt
Northern Vietnamese Rice Balls with Sesame Salt

ingredients: Adjust according to the rice variety.
Remove the papery skin and crush; optional.
preparation_steps: Rinse the rice gently until the water is nearly clear, then drain for about 10 minutes.
Pick through the sesame, prepare shelled roasted peanuts, and dampen a clean cloth or food-safe plastic wrap for shaping.
cooking_steps: Cook the rice with enough water to become soft and sticky but not wet; let it rest for 5 minutes after the cooker switches to warm.
Toast the sesame in a dry pan over low heat, stirring constantly until fragrant and lightly crackling. Pound it with salt and peanuts; add a little sugar if desired.
While the rice is warm, place it on a clean, slightly damp cloth or food-safe wrap. Press and roll firmly into a compact log. Rest for 5–10 minutes to set.
Slice with a slightly wet knife or clean thread and serve with sesame salt.
